content: Slow-release fluoride devices have been studied as a potentially cost-effective method to reduce dental caries, particularly in individuals at high risk for the disease. This review represents the second update of a Cochrane Review originally published in 2006 and updated in 2014. The primary objective of this review was to assess the effectiveness and safety of various types of slow-release fluoride devices in preventing, arresting, or reversing the progression of carious lesions on all surfaces of both primary (deciduous) and permanent teeth. The review involved a comprehensive search of multiple electronic databases, including the Cochrane Oral Health Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and Embase, up to January 23, 2018. Additionally, ongoing trials were identified through ClinicalTrials.gov and the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform. No restrictions were placed on language or publication date during the search process. The inclusion criteria focused on parallel randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared slow-release fluoride devices with alternative fluoride treatments, placebo, or no intervention across all age groups. The primary outcomes of interest were changes in the number of decayed, missing, and filled teeth or surfaces (DMFT/DMFS for permanent teeth and dmft/dmfs for primary teeth) and the progression of carious lesions from enamel into dentine. Standard Cochrane review methods were employed for data collection and analysis. At least two review authors independently screened abstracts, applied inclusion criteria, extracted data, and assessed the risk of bias. Discrepancies were resolved through discussion or arbitration by additional review authors. The review identified no evidence comparing slow-release fluoride devices with other fluoride therapies. Only one double-blind RCT, involving 174 children, met the inclusion criteria. This study compared a slow-release fluoride device (glass beads containing fluoride attached to the buccal surfaces of the right maxillary first permanent molar teeth) with a control device (glass beads without fluoride). The study was conducted in a deprived area with low fluoride levels in drinking water and included children with a mean age of 8.8 years at baseline and 10.9 years at the study's conclusion. At baseline, the children had a DMFT score greater than one and salivary levels of Streptococcus mutans exceeding one million colony-forming units per milliliter. At the two-year follow-up, only 63 children (31 in the intervention group and 32 in the control group) retained the beads, resulting in a retention rate of 47.7%. Among these children, the caries increment was significantly lower in the intervention group compared to the control group. The mean difference in DMFT was -0.72 (95% confidence interval [CI]: -1.23 to -0.21), and the mean difference in DMFS was -1.52 (95% CI: -2.68 to -0.36). However, the quality of this evidence was rated as very low. Importantly, this benefit was only observed in children who retained the fluoride beads, and over 50% of participants did not retain the beads for the full two years. The study did not report any adverse effects or other outcomes of interest, such as the progression of carious lesions, dental pain, or healthcare utilization. The authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence to determine the caries-inhibiting effect of slow-release fluoride glass beads. The available evidence is of very low quality, and the potential benefits may be overestimated for the average child. The findings are not easily generalizable to the broader population, as the study was conducted in a specific high-risk group from a deprived area with low fluoride levels in drinking water. Furthermore, the results were based only on children who retained the beads for two years, and it is unclear whether children who lost the devices earlier derived any benefit.
